claims.claim: Harrison (in comments) states Under Heaven's sections with women viewpoint characters are in present tense while male-viewpoint sections are in past tense.
Harrison quotes the narrator's remark that only a patient historian or a story-shaper would note such conjunctions, as Kay's self-reflexive use of history.
claims.quote: Only a patient historian with access to records

claims.claim: Walton names Kay's Sarantine style an odd, distanced, elegiac 'veiled omniscient': a narrator who knows everything but draws and lifts veils.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)
claims.quote: odd, distanced, elegaic style that I want to call veiled omniscient

claims.claim: Walton dislikes Kay's Dunnett-like trick of describing a character for pages without saying who is who.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)
claims.quote: plays tricks where he described but doesn’t say who is who

claims.claim: Walton says there is always a pulling back, events interpreted through a consciousness of artifice, like the wrong end of a telescope.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)

claims.claim: Walton notes many points of view but Kay never takes up a character just to throw them away; ironic omniscient linking underlines everything.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)
claims.quote: he never takes up a character just to throw them away

claims.claim: Walton observes the books concentrate on single days with heavy flashback, using more pluperfect than anything she can think of, almost like Ulysses.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)
claims.quote: more use of the pluperfect tense in these than anything else

claims.claim: Walton notes a chariot race is seen from a driver, someone in the crowd and an undercook making soup.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)
claims.quote: an undercook for the Blue faction making soup

claims.claim: Walton says Kay mediates the world through chariot races and mosaic-making, describing heresy and empire in those terms.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)
claims.quote: mediates the world through the chariot races

claims.claim: Walton praises details real enough to bite: tesserae quality, mud, fish sauces, the arrow-extraction tool.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)
claims.quote: The details are all real enough to bite

claims.claim: Walton argues renaming reshuffles the deck so no reader knows the ending: a historical novel is inevitably tragedy, a historical fantasy is open.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)

claims.claim: Walton says the little magic runs glinting through everything like silver threads in shot silk.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)
claims.quote: like the silver threads in shot silk

claims.claim: Walton finds Arbonne mannered, distanced and held at arm's length, its world denser than its gossamer characters.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Provencal Fantasy: Guy Gavriel Kay's A Song for Arbonne', Tor.com/Reactor (2010-08-06)
claims.quote: mannered and distanced and held at arm’s length

claims.claim: Walton remembers Arbonne chiefly through set-piece moments of the kind Kay does so well.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Provencal Fantasy: Guy Gavriel Kay's A Song for Arbonne', Tor.com/Reactor (2010-08-06)
claims.quote: a few set-piece moments, of the kind Kay does so well

claims.claim: Walton traces a trajectory away from magic from Fionavar through Tigana and Arbonne to Lions.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Provencal Fantasy: Guy Gavriel Kay's A Song for Arbonne', Tor.com/Reactor (2010-08-06)
